lawyer:
Mr. A.S.M. Nazmul Haque, D.A.G ------ For the appellant. 
Mr. Abdus Salam Mamun with Mrs. Shajeda Aktar Bakul, Advocates ------ For the Respondents No. 3.
parties:
Commissioner of Customs, Customs House (Import), Chittagong
Vs.
The Customs, Excise and Vat Appellate Tribunal and Others
full_judgment:
Nathi No. CEVT/ case (Cus)-891/2010, passed by the Respondent No. 1 disallowing the appeal, thereby affirming the judgment and order of the respondent No. 2, contained in Appeal Order No. 27/2010 dated 10.08.2010. 

 3. The learned Deputy Attorney General Mr. A. S. M. Nazmul Haque along with the learned Assistant Attorneys General Mr. Md. Jahangir Alam Mr. Md. Abdur Rahman Howlader, appearing for the appellant and having placed the Memorandum of appeal, drawn our attention to the paper book and first of all submits that, in this particular case, the PSI agent has rejected the invoice value and issued CRF certificate as per Rule 4 of Valuation Rules, 2000, upon taking into consideration the data base and other materials on record and this was pointed out before the Respondent No. 2. But, the Respondent No. 2 has failed to appreciate that the PSI agent was competent to issue a CRF certificate based on valuation made by it and in that case the assessment of the imported consignment should be done on the base of CRF certificate, instead of invoice value. Besides, the respondent No. 2 (President, Review Committee) has also failed to take into consideration that in respect of many similar consignments imported into Bangladesh, from the same origin as well as from other countries, value was duly determined @US$ 3000.00 to 3002.00 per MT, and the importers in those cases got their consignments released based on such fixed/recorded value without any objection whatsoever. The respondent No. 2, he continues, also did not consider the fact that the Commissioner of Customs is constitutionally empowered to collect the duties/taxes payable on the imported goods. Therefore, lie sums up the order No. 27/10 dated 10.08.2010, passed by the respondent No. 2, is unlawful, based on misconception of facts and law. Thereafter an appeal was preferred before the Tribunal, narrating the relevant facts and placing the case of appellant, with reference to grounds made in the Memo of Appeal. But, the Tribunal has also failed to taken into the consideration the relevant facts and circumstances of the case and acted upon misconstruction of the concerned Rules, and has passed order dated 26.08.2012, contained in Nathi No. CEVT/Case (Cus)-891/2010, whereby it has dismissed the appeal and upheld the judgment and order dated 10.08.2010 passed by the respondent No. 2. He therefore asserts that, the impugned order dated 26.08.2012, passed by the Tribunal, is totally erroneous and based on misconception and misinterpretation of Rules, passed without taking into consideration the relevant materials placed before it. Hence, he sums up that the impugned the appeal is liable to be allowed and that the valuation made by the PSI agent may be upheld by setting aside the impugned judgment and order passed by the Appellate Tribunal. 

 4. The learned advocate Mr. Abdus Salam Mamun, appearing along with learned advocate Ms. Sajada Akter Bakul for the respondent No. 3, on the other hand, submits that in this particular case the importer (respondent No. 3) has submitted all documents along with the concerned Bill of Entry, the Commercial Invoice, the Bill of Lading etc., for the purpose of valuation and clearance of the goods, within due time and according to the procedure laid down in the Act. The documents relating to this particular consignment and were submitted for assement of duties, clearly show the actual price of the goods and the other costs involved in importing the consignment. As such, the customs authority was legally bound to accept the valuation declared in the Bill of Entry that includes the price of the goods and other cost involved in importing the same into Bangladesh. But, he continues, the PSI agent has most arbitrarily and exceeding the authority vested in it, has made an arbitrary valuation of the imported consignment, which was unauthorised and could not be the basis for assessment of the duties. To clarify his submission, the learned advocate has referred to Rule 13 of the Pre-Shipment Inspection Rules, 2002 (PSI Rules, 2002), and submits that sub-rule (1) requires that the customs authority was bound to accept the valuation shown in the Bill of Entry. However, if the valuation declared by the importer has to be increased then sub-rule (2) of Rule 13 of the PSI Rules, 2002, requires that the exporter should be given and opportunity to place his case before the concerned PSI agent, while sub-rule (3) requires that the PSI agent should also procure valuation agreement from the exporter and shall enclose the same with the CRF certificate whereby the valuation is to be increased. But, in the case of this particular consignment, the PSI agent has submitted a CRF certificate showing valuation of the goods @ US$ 3000.70 per MT, whereby it has increased the valuation of goods from US$ 2510.00 per MT, vide CRF No. IT 1059871J dated 27.04.2010. As such, he proceeds on the CRF certificate issued by the PSI agent increasing the valuation of the imported consignment (Milk Powder) from US$ 2510.00 to 3000.70 per MT has been done in clear violation sub-rule (2) and sub-rule (3) of Rule 13 of the PSI Rules, 2002. The learned advocate next referred to sub-rule (4) of Rule 5 of the Valuation Rules, 2000, which stipulates that, if different prices are found in respect of similar goods imported into the Bangladesh, then the lowest price shall be accepted for the purpose of valuation for assessing duties. The learned advocate accordingly emphasises that, from the contemporary data base (from 10.03.2010 to 13.06.2010) it has been found that the same goods (Spray dried Skimmed milk powder) imported from the same country and having same HS Code was released upon valuation @ US$ 2080 to 3030.00 per MT. In that case, as per rule 5(4) of the Valuation Rules, 2000, the lowest price being US$ 2080 per MT should have been accepted for the purpose of valuation of the imported consignment. But, the price declared by the importer is higher than the lowest price thus found. However, the importer (respondent No. 3) under the compelling situation, i.e. to avoid further loss (the goods being perishable), had to release the goods on the valuation shown in the CRF certificate and filed an application before the Review Committee as per rule 23 of the PSI Rules 2002, being aggrieved by the valuation made by the PSI agent. The review committee has considered the proforma invoice, commercial invoice packing list, L.C, Bill of Exchange, certificate of origin, agreement etc. They have also examined the data base from the period 01.012010 to 13.06.2010, as regards the valuation and price of the similar goods for the relevant period and found that similar goods were released at a valuation from US$ 2080.00 to 3030.00 per MT. They have also recorded in their judgment and order No. 27/10 dated 10.08.2010 that, as per Rule 5(4) of valuation Rules, 2000, the importer/respondent No. 3 is entitled to pay duties on the lowest valuation, which is less then that declared by the importer in the Bill of Entry. Accordingly, the Review Committee, instead of directing to pay duty on the lowest valuation, has accepted the valuation declared by the importer at the rate of US$ 2510.00 per MT, which is higher than US$ 2080.00 per MT. The Review Committee has also held that the CRF certificate dated 27.04.2010, fixing valuation of the imported consignment @ US$ 3000.70 per MT, was not in accordance with the rules. Hence, the Review Committee did not accept the same and allowed the review application filed by the importer/respondent No. 3, by a detail and speaking judgment and order and after hearing all the parties. Thereafter, the customs authority preferred an appeal before the Tribunal, he proceeds, being aggrieved by order No. 27/10 dated 10.08.2010 of the Review Committee. The learned advocate for the appellant has taken us through the judgment and order passed by the Tribunal as recorded under reference Nathi No. CEVT/ case (Cus)- 891/2010, dated 26.08.2010, and submits that the Tribunal, by a speaking judgment and order, and giving reasons, as contained in the said judgment and order of the tribunal, has refused the appeal filed by the appellant and affirmed the order No. 27/10 dated 10.08.2010 of the Review Committee. The learned advocate for the respondent No. 3, further submits that, in passing the judgment and order, the Tribunal has taken into consideration all relevant facts, documents, circumstances, the applicable Rules and the Law. As such, he continues, that there is no ground or reason for interference with the judgment and order passed by the Tribunal. Besides, the grounds on which the customs authority has preferred this appeal under section 196D of the Act is devoid of any substance, vague and the grounds taken are totally misconceived. Accordingly, the learned advocate has prayed for dismissing the appeal and to allow the respondent No. 3 to a release the goods on the price declared by the importer in the Bill of Entry and to refund to the duties that will be found to have been realised in excess from the importer, within the time that may be fixed by this court. The learned advocate for the respondent No. 3 has also submitted two unreported judgments, passed in Customs Appeals No. 138 of 2012 and No. 148 of 2012, both filed are under section 196D of the Mt and disposed of analogously by a Bench of this Division on 12.03.2014, dismissed both the appeals, preferred by the Customs Authority, that was decided on similar factual and similar legal issues, and in those two appeals the present appellant was the respondent/importer. 

 9. But, the PSI agent has increased the valuation of the imported goods from USD 2510.00 per MT to USD 3000.70 per MT. In this respect we have consulted Rule 13 of the Pre-Shipment Inspection Rules 2000 (PSI Rules, 2002) and we find that sub-rule (I ) requires that the customs authority is bound to accept the valuation shown in the Bill of Entry. However, if the valuation declared by the importer has to be increased, then sub-rule (2) of Rule 13 of PSI Rules, 2002, requires that the exporter should be given an opportunity to place his case before the concerned PSI agent, while sub-rule (3) requires that the PSI agent should also procure valuation agreement from the exporter and shall enclose the same with the CRF certificate that increases the valuation. But, in the case of this particular consignment, we find that the PSI agent has submitted a CRF certificate showing 'valuation of the goods @ US$ 3000.70 per MT, whereby he has increased the valuation of goods from US$ 2510.00 per MT. vide CRF No. IT 1059871J dated 27.04.2010. But, there is no material on record to show that the provisions sub-Rules (2) or (3) of Rule 13 of the PSI Rules, 2002, was at all complied with by the PSI agent to justify it's act of increasing the valuation from that as declared by the importer. As such, we find that the in issuing CRF No. IT 1059871J the provisions of sub-Rules (1), (2) and (3) of PSI Rules, 2002, has been violated. 

 10. On the other hand, we find that, sub-rule (4) of Rules 5 of Valuation Rules, 2000, which stipulates that if different prices or valuation is found inspect of similar goods imported into Bangladesh, then the lowest price shall be accepted for the purpose of valuation for assessing duties. The data placed on the records shows that similar goods imported from 10.03.2010 to 13.06.201 0 from the same country and under the same HS Code was released upon valuation @ US$ 2080 to 3030.00 per MT. In that case, as per rule 5(4) of valuation Rules, 2000, the lowest price should have been accepted for the purpose of valuation of the imported consignment of the respondent No. 3 (importer). But the price declared by the importer is higher than the lowest price thus found. 

 11. We also find, that in similar two other appeals, a Division Bench of this Division, have considered the similar issues and dismissed both the appeals and that in those two appeals the present respondent No. 3 was the importer. We do not find any reason to depart from the views expressed in those appeals decided on 12.03.2014. We are also of the view, in the facts and circumstances of this case, that the CRF certificate and the valuation declared by the PSI agent was done in clear violation of sub-rule (2) and (3) of Rule 13 of PSI Rules, 2002, and this was done arbitrarily.
